Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

For tests $\varphi_j,\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, $\varphi_j\to\varphi$ in the LF topology if and only if the supports of $\varphi_j$ eventually lie in one compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\partial^\alpha\varphi_j\to\partial^\alpha\varphi$ uniformly on $\Omega$ for every multi-index $\alpha$. Equivalently one compact contains all their supports and that of the limit, and convergence holds in its fixed-support topology. This is a sequence criterion, in ZF.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.
Every continuous map from a nonempty compact Hausdorff space to a uniform space is uniformly continuous.

Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be one-periodic and continuous. Then

$$\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|\sigma_Nf(x)-f(x)|\longrightarrow0 \qquad (N\to\infty).$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For a continuous compactly supported $u:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb C$, write
$u=u_{\mathrm R}+iu_{\mathrm I}$ for its real-coordinate decomposition and
define its complex Riemann integral by
$$\int u:=\int u_{\mathrm R}+i\int u_{\mathrm I},$$
where the real integrals are over a closed rectangle containing the support.
Equivalently, use any sufficiently large cube $[-R,R]^m$; the value stabilizes
as $R$ increases because $u$ vanishes outside its compact support. Each real
component integral exists by
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]. The complex modulus is
$|a+ib|=(a^2+b^2)^{1/2}$; the triangle inequality for Riemann sums gives
$|\int u|\le\int|u|$. Complex linearity and product-rectangle Fubini follow by
applying the real integral rules to the real and imaginary components; in
particular, use [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] componentwise.
Differentiation under a compact parameter integral likewise means applying
[[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]] to both
real components. These conventions apply to every integral below.

Let $d\ge1$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and $n\ge1$. Write
$\mathcal D(X^n)=C_c^\infty(X^n;\mathbb C)$ for the complex test-function
space of smooth compactly supported functions
([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]), with its LF topology
([[def-test-function-topology]]). The convergence criterion used below is
that convergent test sequences have one common compact support and converge
uniformly with every derivative
([[thm-sequential-convergence-in-test-function-space]]). Here $C^\infty$
means every coordinate derivative exists and is continuous
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). All integrals are
compact Riemann integrals: each integrand is continuous with compact support,
so restrict it to a compact rectangle and apply
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]. Let
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$ be the subspace of kernels invariant under
every permutation of their $n$ $X$-variables. Fields are real smooth
configurations $\phi\in C^\infty(X;\mathbb R)$. For an integer $N\ge0$
and a finite family
$f_0\in\mathbb C$, $f_n\in\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$ for
$1\le n\le N$, define
$$ F_f(\phi)=f_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\int_{X^n}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n. $$
The pairing is complex-bilinear, with no conjugation on the kernel or field.
An element of $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$ is this finite symmetric
coefficient family, evaluated on fields by $F_f$. Pointwise sums, scalar
multiples, and products again have finite symmetric compactly supported
coefficient families: for products, expand the two finite sums and
symmetrize each tensor product $f_m\otimes g_n$. Thus these elements form
an algebra; the product-integral identity follows from Riemann Fubini on a
rectangle containing the compact supports
([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]).

For $k=0$, set $F_f^{(0)}(\phi)=F_f(\phi)$. For $1\le k\le N$,
the $k$-th functional derivative kernel assigned to this coefficient
family is
$$ F_f^{(k)}(\phi)(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\sum_{n=k}^{N}\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\int_{X^{n-k}}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_{k+1}\cdots dx_n. $$
For $k>N$ it is zero. Each displayed kernel is smooth, symmetric and compactly supported in its $k$ remaining variables: compactness follows by projection of the finite union of coefficient-kernel supports, and derivatives pass through the finite-compact integrals by [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]].
In the term $n=k$, the empty integral and empty product mean simply
$f_k(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$.

For real smooth directions $h_1,\ldots,h_k$, the pairing of
$F_f^{(k)}(\phi)$ with $h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_k$ is the coefficient of
$t_1\cdots t_k$ in $F_f(\phi+\sum_{j=1}^k t_jh_j)$. For each degree-$n$
term, expanding the finite product assigns the $k$ distinct directions to
the $n$ factors in $n!/(n-k)!$ ways; symmetry of $f_n$ makes the corresponding
integrals equal. This verifies the displayed kernel's functional-derivative
meaning by a finite polynomial calculation.

The scope is exactly smooth compact coefficient kernels. A local functional
whose higher derivative kernels are distributions on a thin diagonal is not
included merely because its field expression is polynomial.

derivations.claim: Fix $\Phi\in\mathcal D(X^n)$ and regard $X^n$ as $\mathbb R^D$, $D=dn$. The coordinate projections of $\operatorname{supp}\Phi$ lie in a compact $K\subset X$. By [F3] choose $\chi\in\mathcal D(X)$ equal to one near $K$. Choose $L>0$ so large that every coordinate of $\operatorname{supp}\chi$ lies strictly inside $(-L/2,L/2)$. Extend $\Phi$ by zero and then $L$-periodically in each of the $D$ coordinates; because its support is interior to the period cube, the resulting function is smooth on the compact $D$-torus.

For $k\in\mathbb Z^D$, put $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i k\cdot x/L)$, $Q=[-L/2,L/2]^D$, and $\widehat\Phi(k)=L^{-D}\int_Q\Phi(x)\overline{e_k(x)}\,dx$. These are Riemann integrals by [F7]. Periodic integration by parts in one coordinate has no boundary term: the endpoint product agrees by periodicity, and [F8] converts the integral of a derivative to that endpoint difference. Writing $\Delta=\sum_{j=1}^D\partial_j^2$, applying this identity to $(1-\Delta)^q\Phi$, and using the character derivative from [F6], gives $\widehat{(1-\Delta)^q\Phi}(k) =(1+(2\pi/L)^2|k|^2)^q\widehat\Phi(k)$. The left side is bounded by the volume of $Q$ times the supremum of the continuous function $(1-\Delta)^q\Phi$, so $$ |\widehat\Phi(k)|\le C_{\Phi,q}\bigl(1+|k|^2\bigr)^{-q}. $$ For integer $m\ge1$, the number of lattice points in $m\le|k|_\infty<m+1$ is at most $(2m+3)^D-(2m-1)^D\le C_D(m+1)^{D-1}$, by expanding the two powers; the shell $|k|_\infty<1$ is finite. Thus, for every multi-index $\alpha$, choosing $q$ with $2q>D+|\alpha|$ makes $\sum_k |k|^{|\alpha|}|\widehat\Phi(k)|$ finite. The Fourier series and each derivative series therefore converge absolutely and uniformly on the torus. Integrating each uniformly convergent derivative series along a coordinate segment and using [F8] shows it is the corresponding derivative of the uniformly convergent Fourier sum; iterating over coordinates gives the same assertion for every multi-index.

The uniform sum has the same Fourier coefficients as $\Phi$, since uniform convergence allows integration term by term and distinct integer characters have zero cross integral by [F6]–[F8]. Their difference is a continuous $D$-periodic function with every multi-index Fourier coefficient zero. For $D=1$, all its Fejer means are finite sums of those zero coefficients, so [F5] makes the function zero. For $D>1$, fix the first frequency $k_1$ and integrate in the first coordinate to obtain a continuous $(D-1)$-periodic coefficient function; continuity follows from [F4] and the compact integral bound [F7]. Its remaining Fourier coefficients are the corresponding coefficients of the original difference by [F7], so induction makes each such coefficient function zero. Applying the one-dimensional case to each fixed choice of the remaining coordinates shows the original difference is zero. Hence the Fourier series sums to $\Phi$, with all derivatives uniformly.

Let $S_M\Phi$ be the finite Fourier sum over $|k|_\infty\le M$. On $\mathbb R^D$, put $$ P_M(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\chi(x_j)\right)S_M\Phi(x_1,\ldots,x_n). $$ Each Fourier character factors over the $n$ blocks $x_j\in\mathbb R^d$; after multiplication by the product cutoff, each term is an elementary tensor of tests in $\mathcal D(X)$. Also $(\prod_j\chi(x_j))\Phi=\Phi$, since every coordinate projection of its support lies in $K$. The product rule [F8] and the derivative convergence from step 2.1 show $P_M\to\Phi$ uniformly with every derivative, with all supports in the fixed compact $(\operatorname{supp}\chi)^n$. By [F1] this is convergence in the LF topology. Applying the finite symmetrization operator preserves convergence and turns the approximants into symmetric finite tensor sums whenever $\Phi$ is symmetric.

Suppose $\sum_{n=0}^{N}\int f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_j\phi(x_j)\,dx=0$ for every real smooth $\phi$, with symmetric test kernels $f_n$ as in [F9]. Replacing $\phi$ by $t\phi$ makes a scalar polynomial in $t$ vanish for every real $t$, so each homogeneous term $\int f_n\phi^{\otimes n}$ is zero for every $\phi$. For fixed real test functions $h_1,\ldots,h_n$, substitute $\phi=\sum_j t_jh_j$. The coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_n$ is $n!\int f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_jh_j(x_j)\,dx$, by symmetry, and must vanish. Complex product tests are finite linear combinations of real product tests by separating real and imaginary parts. Step 3.1 makes their span dense, so choose approximants $\psi_M\to\overline{f_n}$ with support in a fixed compact rectangle $C$. The componentwise convention [F7, F9] and the Riemann-sum triangle inequality give $$ \left|\int f_n(\psi_M-\overline{f_n})\right| \le \operatorname{vol}(C)\|f_n\|_\infty \|\psi_M-\overline{f_n}\|_\infty\longrightarrow0. $$ Thus $\int|f_n|^2=0$. If $f_n$ were nonzero at some point, its support constraint and continuity give a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subset\operatorname{int}C$ and $c>0$ with $|f_n|\ge c$ on $Q$. Insert the faces of $Q$ into a Darboux grid of $C$. Since $|f_n|^2\ge0$ everywhere and $|f_n|^2\ge c^2$ on $Q$, the lower Darboux sum is at least $c^2\operatorname{vol}(Q)>0$, so the real Riemann integral is positive, a contradiction. Hence $f_n=0$. The constant term is zero by taking $\phi=0$. This proves uniqueness and the well-definedness claim used by the definition.

$$\Delta_\mu(f,g)= \int_{\mathbb R^4}\!\int_{\mathbb R^4} f(x)g(y)\Delta_\mu(x-y)\,d^4x\,d^4y.$$
On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the smeared fields of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]] satisfy
$$[\Phi_\mu(f),\Phi_\mu(g)]=-i\Delta_\mu(f,g)I.$$
Consequently spacelike-separated supports give commuting fields.

Set $X=\mathbb R^4$. Fix $\mu\ge0$ and the $(-+++)$, shell, Fourier, and coordinate conventions
of [[lem-qft-free-time-ordered-kernel]]. That current supplier states that
its relative-coordinate tempered distribution $H_\mu$ is symmetric, agrees
with the ordered Wightman kernels on strictly ordered time supports and on
spacelike-separated supports, and has no prefactor $i$ in its definition.
Its current carrier is a draft with a supplied conditional proof; the formula
below uses that exact interface. Complex integrals of compactly supported
regular kernels use the componentwise Riemann convention in
[[def-qft-regular-polynomial-functional-algebra]]: write the integrand as its
real part plus $i$ times its imaginary part and integrate each real component.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is the space
of smooth compactly supported complex tests with the LF topology, and
$\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ is its continuous complex-linear dual, paired
bilinearly with no conjugation
([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-test-function-topology]],
[[def-distribution]]). Schwartz space consists of smooth functions with all
polynomially weighted derivatives bounded; $\mathcal S'$ is its continuous
complex-linear dual with bilinear pairing
([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]],
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]], [[def-tempered-distribution]]).

For any relative-coordinate distribution $K\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^4)$,
define its translation-invariant two-point bidistribution
$\widetilde K\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4)$ by
$$ \langle\widetilde K,\Psi\rangle =\left\langle K,\ z\longmapsto\int_{\mathbb R^4}\Psi(y+z,y)\,dy\right\rangle, \qquad \Psi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4). $$
The inner function is a test function: its support lies in the difference
of the two compact coordinate projections of $\operatorname{supp}\Psi$;
each derivative in $z$ is the Riemann integral of the corresponding
first-variable derivative of $\Psi$ over a compact rectangle containing
the fixed compact second-variable projection; iterate the real
single-coordinate differentiation rule over every derivative in $z$ and
apply it to both real components, using the compact parameter-integral
differentiation convention of
[[def-qft-regular-polynomial-functional-algebra]].
On each fixed compact support space, every output derivative seminorm is
bounded by the volume of a compact rectangle containing the second-variable
projection times the corresponding source derivative seminorm. The support
of the output lies in the compact difference of the two projections. Thus
this map is continuous on each fixed-support test space, and hence on the LF
test topology [[def-test-function-topology]].
Thus the displayed formula defines a distribution without multiplying
singular distributions. Write $\mathsf H_\mu=\widetilde H_\mu$.

For $F\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbb R^4)$, define its support as the
finite union of the coordinate projections of the supports of its nonconstant
symmetric coefficient kernels. This is a compact set and is presentation
independent by [[lem-qft-tensor-test-function-density]]. For compact
$A,B\subset\mathbb R^4$, write $A\succcurlyeq_{\mathrm{out}} B$ when
$$ x-y\notin C_-:=\{(t,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4:t\le-|\mathbf x|\} \quad\text{for every }x\in A,\ y\in B. $$
This means the first support has no point in the closed causal past of the
second, using the supplier's fixed inertial chart.

For $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal Q_n$ consist of finite coefficient families in
$n$ independent real smooth fields $\phi_i\in C^\infty(X;\mathbb R)$ of the form
$$Q(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n)=\sum_{\mathbf r}\int q_{\mathbf r}(\mathbf x^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf x^{(n)})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{a=1}^{r_i}\phi_i(x_a^{(i)})\,d\mathbf x,$$
where $\mathbf r=(r_1,\ldots,r_n)\in\mathbb N_0^n$ ranges over a finite set,
$q_{\mathbf r}\in C_c^\infty(X^{r_1}\times\cdots\times X^{r_n};\mathbb C)$,
and each coefficient is symmetric within every block
$\mathbf x^{(i)}=(x_1^{(i)},\ldots,x_{r_i}^{(i)})$.
$X^0$ is a one-point space; an empty product and an integral over no variables
leave the scalar coefficient unchanged. Here $d\mathbf x$ is the product of
the $d^4x_a^{(i)}$ coordinate volume elements over all variables present.
The product
$\prod_iF_i(\phi_i)$ of regular polynomials is in $\mathcal Q_n$.

For $1\le i<j\le n$, define the one-pair contraction
$D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}:\mathcal Q_n\to\mathcal Q_n$ linearly and termwise on
each block coefficient $q_{\mathbf r}$. It is zero if $r_i=0$ or $r_j=0$;
otherwise it has multidegree $\mathbf r-\mathbf e_i-\mathbf e_j$ and
coefficient
$$q'_{\mathbf r-\mathbf e_i-\mathbf e_j}(\mathbf x')=r_i r_j\left\langle\mathsf H_\mu,(x,y)\longmapsto q_{\mathbf r}(\ldots,x,\ldots,y,\ldots)\right\rangle,$$
where $x$ occupies the first variable of block $i$, $y$ occupies the first
variable of block $j$, and the uncontracted variables $\mathbf x'$ are held
as parameters. The result remains symmetric within each remaining block.
The parameter-pairing theorem
[[lem-distribution-pairing-with-smooth-parameter-families]] makes this
coefficient smooth and compactly supported. The factor $r_i r_j$ counts the
choices of one variable from each symmetric block, so this is exactly one
functional derivative in each of the independent field slots followed by
pairing against $\mathsf H_\mu$.

For $r\ge1$, define full symmetrization by
$$\operatorname{Sym}_r h(x_1,\ldots,x_r)=\frac1{r!}\sum_{\pi\in S_r}h(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(r)}),$$
with $\operatorname{Sym}_0$ the identity. For $Q\in\mathcal Q_n$, define
$m_nQ$ by setting $\phi_1=\cdots=\phi_n=\phi$ and replacing each remaining
block coefficient by its full symmetrization across all variables. For a finite-degree $Q$, the
formal exponential is defined coefficientwise by
$$\exp\!\left(\eta\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}\right)Q =\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{\eta^r}{r!}\left(\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}\right)^rQ,$$
which terminates because each contraction lowers total degree by two. The
parameter $\eta$ is formal and fixed by complex conjugation. Define
$$ T_n^H(F_1,\ldots,F_n)(\phi) =m_n\exp\!\left(\eta\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}\right) \prod_{i=1}^nF_i(\phi_i), \qquad T_0^H=1,\quad T_1^H(F)=F. $$
The tensor-product distribution theorem
[[thm-tensor-product-distributions-and-iterated-pairings]] and the
parameter-pairing theorem above make every contraction well defined; no
diagonal product occurs. Symmetry of $\mathsf H_\mu$ makes $T_n^H$ symmetric
in its inputs.

For any $V\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbb R^4)$ and formal coupling $z$,
define
$$ S_z^H(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(iz/\eta)^n}{n!}\,T_n^H(V,\ldots,V) \quad\text{with coefficients in }\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbb R^4)[\eta,\eta^{-1}]. $$
This is a coefficientwise formal series; the definition asserts no
convergence in $z$, no time-ordered product for singular local functionals,
and no continuum interacting field.

Let $X=\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and let $W\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ be
any continuous complex bidistribution. For a real formal parameter $\eta$
and $F,G\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$, define
$$ F\star_W G=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\eta^k}{k!}\left\langle W^{\otimes k},F^{(k)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(k)}(\phi)\right\rangle . $$
The pairing is over $k$ independent pairs of variables; $W^{\otimes k}$
is formed by iterated distributional tensor products, not by multiplying
distributions at coincident points. The sum is finite because the inputs are
polynomial. It defines an element of
$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$, and $\star_W$ is associative.
Here complex conjugation is $\overline{a+ib}=a-ib$ for $a,b\in\mathbb R$.
If $W$ is Hermitian in the sense
$\overline{\langle W,\overline g\otimes\overline f\rangle}
=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle$, then
$(F\star_W G)^*=G^*\star_W F^*$, where $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$.
For $\ell_f(\phi)=\int_X f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$,
$$ [\ell_f,\ell_g]_{\star_W}=\eta\bigl(W(f,g)-W(g,f)\bigr), \qquad W(f,g):=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle . $$

Let $d,n\ge1$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and give
$\mathcal D(X^n)=C_c^\infty(X^n;\mathbb C)$ its LF test-function topology.
The finite linear span of elementary product tests
$$ (x_1,\ldots,x_n)\longmapsto\prod_{j=1}^{n}g_j(x_j),\qquad g_j\in\mathcal D(X), $$
is dense. More precisely, for each $\Phi\in\mathcal D(X^n)$, there is a
sequence of such finite sums whose supports lie in one fixed compact product
and whose derivatives of every multi-index converge uniformly to those of
$\Phi$. Symmetrized finite sums are dense in
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$. Consequently the symmetric-kernel
representation in [[def-qft-regular-polynomial-functional-algebra]] is
unique: if a finite symmetric-kernel polynomial vanishes on every real smooth
field, every coefficient kernel vanishes.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $v\in\mathcal D'(V)$ the tensor candidate is a distribution on $U\times V$, uniquely determined by $(u\otimes v)(\varphi\otimes\psi)=u(\varphi)v(\psi)$. Its two iterated pairing orders agree, and $\operatorname{supp}(u\otimes v)=\operatorname{supp}u\times\operatorname{supp}v$. Three-factor pairings associate. Moreover $\partial_x^\alpha(u\otimes v)=(\partial^\alpha u)\otimes v$ and $\partial_y^\beta(u\otimes v)=u\otimes(\partial^\beta v)$. All claims hold in ZF.

derivations.claim: Taking vacuum expectations in the commutator of [F3] and using the covariance in [F2] gives $W_\mu(f,g)-W_\mu(g,f)=-i\Delta_\mu(f,g)$ for real compact tests. Complex bilinearity extends this equality to complex product tests, and density [F6] extends it to the lifted bidistributions: $\widetilde W_\mu-\widetilde W_\mu^{\mathsf T}=-i\widetilde\Delta_\mu$. If $\Psi$ is supported where $x-y$ is spacelike, the relative test $z\mapsto\int\Psi(y+z,y)\,dy$ is compactly supported in the spacelike open set. By [F3] its pairing with $\Delta_\mu$ is zero. Thus $\widetilde W_\mu-\widetilde W_\mu^{\mathsf T}$ vanishes there. The conclusion is conditional on the current QFT-MF02 statements.

Put $C=A-B$. Every $z=x-y\in C$ either has $z^0>0$ or is spacelike: if $z^0\le0$ and it is not spacelike, then $z\in C_-$, excluded by $A\succcurlyeq_{\mathrm{out}}B$; this also excludes the zero difference. Thus $C$ lies in the open set $\Omega=U_+\cup U_{\mathrm{sp}}$, where $U_+=\{z:z^0>0\}$ and $U_{\mathrm{sp}}=\{z:(z^0)^2-|\mathbf z|^2<0\}$. By [F7], the cover $\{U_+,U_{\mathrm{sp}}\}$ of $\Omega$ has a locally finite smooth partition of unity subordinate to these sets. Any compactly supported relative test in $\Omega$ meets only finitely many partition functions. On each $U_+$ piece [F1] gives $H_\mu=W_\mu$; on each $U_{\mathrm{sp}}$ piece [F1] gives agreement with both Wightman orderings, which coincide there by step 1.1. Therefore $\widetilde H_\mu-\widetilde W_\mu$ vanishes on $\Omega$. The open set $O=\{(x,y):x-y\in\Omega\}$ contains $A\times B$, and the lift [F4] sends every test supported in $O$ to a relative test supported in $\Omega$. Hence $\widetilde H_\mu-\widetilde W_\mu$ vanishes on an open neighborhood of $A\times B$.

For any finite number $r$ of cross pairs, expand $\widetilde H_\mu^{\otimes r}-\widetilde W_\mu^{\otimes r}$ by telescoping; each summand contains one factor $\widetilde H_\mu-\widetilde W_\mu$. Its support is disjoint from the corresponding open neighborhood of $A\times B$ by [F8] and step 2.1, so it pairs to zero with derivative-kernel tests supported in $(A\times B)^r$. Therefore every finite cross contraction is unchanged when the time-ordered kernel is replaced by $W_\mu$.

In the finite contraction formula for $T_{p+q}^H(\underbrace{V,\ldots,V}_{p\text{ inputs}}, \underbrace{U,\ldots,U}_{q\text{ inputs}})$, split $\sum_{i<j}D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}$ into contractions within the first $p$ slots, within the last $q$ slots, and between the two blocks. Two such operators may share a field block, but they contract distinct variable copies. If they share block $i$, symmetry of its coefficient kernel lets one exchange the labels of the two contracted variables; the tensor-product pairings then agree in either order by [F8]. Thus the within-first, within-last, and cross-block sums commute. Their first two exponentials give $T_p^H(V,\ldots,V)$ and $T_q^H(U,\ldots,U)$. By the finite product rule on the block coefficients, the $r$-th term of the cross-block exponential is $\eta^r/r!$ times the independent $r$-pair contraction of the $r$-th derivative kernels of these two block outputs. After replacing the cross kernels by $W_\mu$ using step 3.1, this is exactly the finite star-product formula [F5]. Every remaining field variable comes from an original coefficient kernel, so within-block contractions retain support in $A$ or $B$. Hence $$ T_{p+q}^H(\underbrace{V,\ldots,V}_{p\text{ inputs}}, \underbrace{U,\ldots,U}_{q\text{ inputs}})=T_p^H(V,\ldots,V)\star_{W_\mu}T_q^H(U,\ldots,U). $$ For $p=0$ or $q=0$, the empty block is $T_0^H=1$ and the same identity follows directly.

In the degree-$n$ coefficient of $S_z^H(V+U)$, symmetry of $T_n^H$ groups terms with $p$ copies of $V$ and $q$ copies of $U$, $p+q=n$, with factor $\binom{n}{p}$. Dividing by $n!$ gives $1/(p!q!)$. Substitution of step 4.1 therefore gives exactly the degree-$n$ coefficient of $S_z^H(V)\star_{W_\mu}S_z^H(U)$. Since $n$ was arbitrary, the causal-factorization identity holds coefficientwise, with no convergence in $z$.

If $A,B$ are pairwise spacelike separated, step 1.1 gives $\widetilde W_\mu=\widetilde W_\mu^{\mathsf T}$ on $A\times B$. Swapping the two inputs in the finite $\star_{W_\mu}$ formula reverses each cross pairing and changes no within-input term, so $F\star_{W_\mu}G=G\star_{W_\mu}F$. Applying this coefficientwise to the formal series proves their commutation.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. Write

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

This is a subspace of the vector space $\mathcal L(X,Y)$ of
[[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], with the same pointwise operations:

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

If $X=Y$, write

$$\mathcal B(X) := \mathcal B(X,X).$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let

The identity operator has norm at most one, including when $\mathcal H=\{0\}$. For a continuous compactly supported $u:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb C$, write
$u=u_{\mathrm R}+iu_{\mathrm I}$ for its real-coordinate decomposition and
define its complex Riemann integral by
$$\int u:=\int u_{\mathrm R}+i\int u_{\mathrm I},$$
where the real integrals are over a closed rectangle containing the support.
Equivalently, use any sufficiently large cube $[-R,R]^m$; the value stabilizes
as $R$ increases because $u$ vanishes outside its compact support. Each real
component integral exists by
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]. The complex modulus is
$|a+ib|=(a^2+b^2)^{1/2}$; the triangle inequality for Riemann sums gives
$|\int u|\le\int|u|$. Complex linearity and product-rectangle Fubini follow by
applying the real integral rules to the real and imaginary components; in
particular, use [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] componentwise.
Differentiation under a compact parameter integral likewise means applying
[[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]] to both
real components. These conventions apply to every integral below.

Let $d\ge1$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and $n\ge1$. Write
$\mathcal D(X^n)=C_c^\infty(X^n;\mathbb C)$ for the complex test-function
space of smooth compactly supported functions
([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]), with its LF topology
([[def-test-function-topology]]). The convergence criterion used below is
that convergent test sequences have one common compact support and converge
uniformly with every derivative
([[thm-sequential-convergence-in-test-function-space]]). Here $C^\infty$
means every coordinate derivative exists and is continuous
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). All integrals are
compact Riemann integrals: each integrand is continuous with compact support,
so restrict it to a compact rectangle and apply
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]. Let
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$ be the subspace of kernels invariant under
every permutation of their $n$ $X$-variables. Fields are real smooth
configurations $\phi\in C^\infty(X;\mathbb R)$. For an integer $N\ge0$
and a finite family
$f_0\in\mathbb C$, $f_n\in\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$ for
$1\le n\le N$, define
$$ F_f(\phi)=f_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\int_{X^n}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n. $$
The pairing is complex-bilinear, with no conjugation on the kernel or field.
An element of $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$ is this finite symmetric
coefficient family, evaluated on fields by $F_f$. Pointwise sums, scalar
multiples, and products again have finite symmetric compactly supported
coefficient families: for products, expand the two finite sums and
symmetrize each tensor product $f_m\otimes g_n$. Thus these elements form
an algebra; the product-integral identity follows from Riemann Fubini on a
rectangle containing the compact supports
([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]).

For $k=0$, set $F_f^{(0)}(\phi)=F_f(\phi)$. For $1\le k\le N$,
the $k$-th functional derivative kernel assigned to this coefficient
family is
$$ F_f^{(k)}(\phi)(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\sum_{n=k}^{N}\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\int_{X^{n-k}}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_{k+1}\cdots dx_n. $$
For $k>N$ it is zero. Each displayed kernel is smooth, symmetric and compactly supported in its $k$ remaining variables: compactness follows by projection of the finite union of coefficient-kernel supports, and derivatives pass through the finite-compact integrals by [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]].
In the term $n=k$, the empty integral and empty product mean simply
$f_k(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$.

For real smooth directions $h_1,\ldots,h_k$, the pairing of
$F_f^{(k)}(\phi)$ with $h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_k$ is the coefficient of
$t_1\cdots t_k$ in $F_f(\phi+\sum_{j=1}^k t_jh_j)$. For each degree-$n$
term, expanding the finite product assigns the $k$ distinct directions to
the $n$ factors in $n!/(n-k)!$ ways; symmetry of $f_n$ makes the corresponding
integrals equal. This verifies the displayed kernel's functional-derivative
meaning by a finite polynomial calculation.

The scope is exactly smooth compact coefficient kernels. A local functional
whose higher derivative kernels are distributions on a thin diagonal is not
included merely because its field expression is polynomial.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

Let $X=\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and let $W\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ be
any continuous complex bidistribution. For a real formal parameter $\eta$
and $F,G\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$, define
$$ F\star_W G=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\eta^k}{k!}\left\langle W^{\otimes k},F^{(k)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(k)}(\phi)\right\rangle . $$
The pairing is over $k$ independent pairs of variables; $W^{\otimes k}$
is formed by iterated distributional tensor products, not by multiplying
distributions at coincident points. The sum is finite because the inputs are
polynomial. It defines an element of
$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$, and $\star_W$ is associative.
Here complex conjugation is $\overline{a+ib}=a-ib$ for $a,b\in\mathbb R$.
If $W$ is Hermitian in the sense
$\overline{\langle W,\overline g\otimes\overline f\rangle}
=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle$, then
$(F\star_W G)^*=G^*\star_W F^*$, where $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$.
For $\ell_f(\phi)=\int_X f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$,
$$ [\ell_f,\ell_g]_{\star_W}=\eta\bigl(W(f,g)-W(g,f)\bigr), \qquad W(f,g):=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle . $$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, say $u$ **vanishes on** an open $V\subseteq\Omega$ if its restriction to $V$ is zero. Let $Z$ be the union of all such open sets. Locality in [[thm-distributions-form-a-sheaf]] shows that $u|_Z=0$, since these sets cover $Z$ and all its restrictions are zero. Thus $Z$ is the largest vanishing open set. The **support** is the relatively closed set $\operatorname{supp}u=\Omega\setminus Z$.

In particular $\operatorname{supp}u=\varnothing$ if and only if $u=0$: emptiness gives $Z=\Omega$ and vanishing there, while the zero distribution vanishes everywhere. If a test $\varphi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$, its compact support is contained in $Z$, so $u(\varphi)=0$ by restriction. Consequently two tests agreeing on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$ have equal pairings with $u$, by applying this fact to their difference.

**Compactly supported** means that $\operatorname{supp}u$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Relative closedness in an arbitrary open domain is not by itself compactness or closedness in the ambient Euclidean space. On the empty domain support is empty. The union and locality argument require no selection of vanishing neighborhoods and no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Define $d_X:X\to X\times X$ by $d_X(x)=(x,x)$. For $\Psi\in\mathcal D(X\times X)$, the diagonal restriction $x\mapsto\Psi(d_X(x))$ has first derivatives $\partial_{x_j}\Psi(x,x)+\partial_{y_j}\Psi(x,x)$ by [F2]. Iterating this formula on the smooth partial derivatives of $\Psi$ shows the restriction has continuous derivatives of every order, so it is smooth. Its support is contained in the first-coordinate projection of $\operatorname{supp}\Psi$, which is compact as a continuous image of a compact set. The componentwise convention in the Statement and [F3] make the displayed integral well defined.

The assignment is complex-linear. Fix a nonempty compact $K\subseteq X\times X$ and a compact rectangle $R\subseteq X$ containing its first-coordinate projection. For every $\Psi$ supported in $K$, $$ |\langle\delta_{\Delta_X},\Psi\rangle| \le \operatorname{vol}(R)\sup_{(x,y)\in K}|\Psi(x,y)|. $$ Thus the seminorm $q(\Psi)=|\langle\delta_{\Delta_X},\Psi\rangle|$ is continuous on every fixed-support test space. By the LF topology definition in [F1], such seminorms are continuous on $\mathcal D(X\times X)$. Therefore $\delta_{\Delta_X}\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$.

If an open set $U\subseteq X\times X$ is disjoint from $\Delta_X$, then every test supported in $U$ vanishes at every $(x,x)$. Its pairing with $\delta_{\Delta_X}$ is zero, so [F5] gives $\operatorname{supp}\delta_{\Delta_X}\subseteq\Delta_X$.

Fix $(x_0,x_0)\in\Delta_X$ and any open neighborhood $U$ of this point. There is a ball $B$ about $x_0$ with $\overline B\times\overline B\subseteq U$. By [F4] choose $h\in\mathcal D(X)$ with $h\ge0$, $h(x_0)=1$, and support in $B$. By continuity choose a closed nondegenerate cube $Q$ inside $B$ on which $h\ge1/2$, and choose a sufficiently large cube $R$ containing $\operatorname{supp}h$ and $Q$ with the faces of $Q$ among its grid cuts. The lower Darboux sum of the nonnegative function $h^2$ on this grid is at least $\operatorname{vol}(Q)/4>0$, so its real Riemann integral is positive. The product test $\Psi(x,y)=h(x)h(y)$ is supported in $U$, and $\langle\delta_{\Delta_X},\Psi\rangle=\int_X h(x)^2\,d^4x>0$. Thus $\delta_{\Delta_X}$ does not vanish on any neighborhood of $(x_0,x_0)$, so $(x_0,x_0)\in\operatorname{supp}\delta_{\Delta_X}$ by [F5]. Since the point was arbitrary, $\Delta_X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\delta_{\Delta_X}$. Together with step 3.1 this gives equality.

For every $\Psi$, the diagonal restrictions of $\Psi(x,y)$ and $\Psi(y,x)$ coincide, so the distribution is symmetric. The diagonal has empty interior: every product neighborhood of a point $(x,x)$ contains $(x,y)$ with $y\ne x$. If a smooth function supported on the diagonal were nonzero at a point, continuity would make it nonzero on an open neighborhood, contradicting empty interior. Therefore every such smooth function is zero.
