For a continuous compactly supported $u:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb C$, write
$u=u_{\mathrm R}+iu_{\mathrm I}$ for its real-coordinate decomposition and
define its complex Riemann integral by
$$\int u:=\int u_{\mathrm R}+i\int u_{\mathrm I},$$
where the real integrals are over a closed rectangle containing the support.
Equivalently, use any sufficiently large cube $[-R,R]^m$; the value stabilizes
as $R$ increases because $u$ vanishes outside its compact support. Each real
component integral exists by
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]. The complex modulus is
$|a+ib|=(a^2+b^2)^{1/2}$; the triangle inequality for Riemann sums gives
$|\int u|\le\int|u|$. Complex linearity and product-rectangle Fubini follow by
applying the real integral rules to the real and imaginary components; in
particular, use [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] componentwise.
Differentiation under a compact parameter integral likewise means applying
[[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]] to both
real components. These conventions apply to every integral below.

Let $d\ge1$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and $n\ge1$. Write
$\mathcal D(X^n)=C_c^\infty(X^n;\mathbb C)$ for the complex test-function
space of smooth compactly supported functions
([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]), with its LF topology
([[def-test-function-topology]]). The convergence criterion used below is
that convergent test sequences have one common compact support and converge
uniformly with every derivative
([[thm-sequential-convergence-in-test-function-space]]). Here $C^\infty$
means every coordinate derivative exists and is continuous
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). All integrals are
compact Riemann integrals: each integrand is continuous with compact support,
so restrict it to a compact rectangle and apply
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]. Let
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$ be the subspace of kernels invariant under
every permutation of their $n$ $X$-variables. Fields are real smooth
configurations $\phi\in C^\infty(X;\mathbb R)$. For an integer $N\ge0$
and a finite family
$f_0\in\mathbb C$, $f_n\in\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$ for
$1\le n\le N$, define
$$ F_f(\phi)=f_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N}\int_{X^n}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n. $$
The pairing is complex-bilinear, with no conjugation on the kernel or field.
An element of $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$ is this finite symmetric
coefficient family, evaluated on fields by $F_f$. Pointwise sums, scalar
multiples, and products again have finite symmetric compactly supported
coefficient families: for products, expand the two finite sums and
symmetrize each tensor product $f_m\otimes g_n$. Thus these elements form
an algebra; the product-integral identity follows from Riemann Fubini on a
rectangle containing the compact supports
([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]).

For $k=0$, set $F_f^{(0)}(\phi)=F_f(\phi)$. For $1\le k\le N$,
the $k$-th functional derivative kernel assigned to this coefficient
family is
$$ F_f^{(k)}(\phi)(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\sum_{n=k}^{N}\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\int_{X^{n-k}}f_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n}\phi(x_j)\,dx_{k+1}\cdots dx_n. $$
For $k>N$ it is zero. Each displayed kernel is smooth, symmetric and compactly supported in its $k$ remaining variables: compactness follows by projection of the finite union of coefficient-kernel supports, and derivatives pass through the finite-compact integrals by [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]].
In the term $n=k$, the empty integral and empty product mean simply
$f_k(x_1,\ldots,x_k)$.

For real smooth directions $h_1,\ldots,h_k$, the pairing of
$F_f^{(k)}(\phi)$ with $h_1\otimes\cdots\otimes h_k$ is the coefficient of
$t_1\cdots t_k$ in $F_f(\phi+\sum_{j=1}^k t_jh_j)$. For each degree-$n$
term, expanding the finite product assigns the $k$ distinct directions to
the $n$ factors in $n!/(n-k)!$ ways; symmetry of $f_n$ makes the corresponding
integrals equal. This verifies the displayed kernel's functional-derivative
meaning by a finite polynomial calculation.

The scope is exactly smooth compact coefficient kernels. A local functional
whose higher derivative kernels are distributions on a thin diagonal is not
included merely because its field expression is polynomial.

Let $d,n\ge1$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and give
$\mathcal D(X^n)=C_c^\infty(X^n;\mathbb C)$ its LF test-function topology.
The finite linear span of elementary product tests
$$ (x_1,\ldots,x_n)\longmapsto\prod_{j=1}^{n}g_j(x_j),\qquad g_j\in\mathcal D(X), $$
is dense. More precisely, for each $\Phi\in\mathcal D(X^n)$, there is a
sequence of such finite sums whose supports lie in one fixed compact product
and whose derivatives of every multi-index converge uniformly to those of
$\Phi$. Symmetrized finite sums are dense in
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{sym}}(X^n)$. Consequently the symmetric-kernel
representation in [[def-qft-regular-polynomial-functional-algebra]] is
unique: if a finite symmetric-kernel polynomial vanishes on every real smooth
field, every coefficient kernel vanishes.

Let $X=\mathbb R^4$ and let $\Delta_X=\{(x,y)\in X\times X:x=y\}$.
For a continuous compactly supported $u:X\to\mathbb C$, write
$u=u_{\mathrm R}+iu_{\mathrm I}$ and define $\int_Xu$ as the stabilized
componentwise real Riemann integral over cubes $[-R,R]^4$ containing
$\operatorname{supp}u$. The real component integrals exist by
[[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]; additivity of real
Riemann sums shows the value is independent of the sufficiently large cube.
Use $|a+ib|=(a^2+b^2)^{1/2}$ for the complex modulus. The Riemann-sum
triangle inequality gives $|\int_Xu|\le\int_X|u|$.
For $\Psi\in\mathcal D(X\times X)$, define
$$ \langle\delta_{\Delta_X},\Psi\rangle =\int_X\Psi(x,x)\,d^4x. $$
Then $\delta_{\Delta_X}\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ is a continuous
complex-linear distribution with support exactly $\Delta_X$, and it is
symmetric under exchanging $x$ and $y$. No nonzero smooth function on
$X\times X$ is supported on $\Delta_X$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, say $u$ **vanishes on** an open $V\subseteq\Omega$ if its restriction to $V$ is zero. Let $Z$ be the union of all such open sets. Locality in [[thm-distributions-form-a-sheaf]] shows that $u|_Z=0$, since these sets cover $Z$ and all its restrictions are zero. Thus $Z$ is the largest vanishing open set. The **support** is the relatively closed set $\operatorname{supp}u=\Omega\setminus Z$.

In particular $\operatorname{supp}u=\varnothing$ if and only if $u=0$: emptiness gives $Z=\Omega$ and vanishing there, while the zero distribution vanishes everywhere. If a test $\varphi$ vanishes on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$, its compact support is contained in $Z$, so $u(\varphi)=0$ by restriction. Consequently two tests agreeing on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}u$ have equal pairings with $u$, by applying this fact to their difference.

**Compactly supported** means that $\operatorname{supp}u$ is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Relative closedness in an arbitrary open domain is not by itself compactness or closedness in the ambient Euclidean space. On the empty domain support is empty. The union and locality argument require no selection of vanishing neighborhoods and no choice axiom.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.

Let $X=\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and let $W\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ be
any continuous complex bidistribution. For a real formal parameter $\eta$
and $F,G\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$, define
$$ F\star_W G=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\eta^k}{k!}\left\langle W^{\otimes k},F^{(k)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(k)}(\phi)\right\rangle . $$
The pairing is over $k$ independent pairs of variables; $W^{\otimes k}$
is formed by iterated distributional tensor products, not by multiplying
distributions at coincident points. The sum is finite because the inputs are
polynomial. It defines an element of
$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$, and $\star_W$ is associative.
Here complex conjugation is $\overline{a+ib}=a-ib$ for $a,b\in\mathbb R$.
If $W$ is Hermitian in the sense
$\overline{\langle W,\overline g\otimes\overline f\rangle}
=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle$, then
$(F\star_W G)^*=G^*\star_W F^*$, where $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$.
For $\ell_f(\phi)=\int_X f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$,
$$ [\ell_f,\ell_g]_{\star_W}=\eta\bigl(W(f,g)-W(g,f)\bigr), \qquad W(f,g):=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle . $$

Set $X=\mathbb R^4$. Fix $\mu\ge0$ and the $(-+++)$, shell, Fourier, and coordinate conventions
of [[lem-qft-free-time-ordered-kernel]]. That current supplier states that
its relative-coordinate tempered distribution $H_\mu$ is symmetric, agrees
with the ordered Wightman kernels on strictly ordered time supports and on
spacelike-separated supports, and has no prefactor $i$ in its definition.
Its current carrier is a draft with a supplied conditional proof; the formula
below uses that exact interface. Complex integrals of compactly supported
regular kernels use the componentwise Riemann convention in
[[def-qft-regular-polynomial-functional-algebra]]: write the integrand as its
real part plus $i$ times its imaginary part and integrate each real component.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is the space
of smooth compactly supported complex tests with the LF topology, and
$\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ is its continuous complex-linear dual, paired
bilinearly with no conjugation
([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-test-function-topology]],
[[def-distribution]]). Schwartz space consists of smooth functions with all
polynomially weighted derivatives bounded; $\mathcal S'$ is its continuous
complex-linear dual with bilinear pairing
([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]],
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]], [[def-tempered-distribution]]).

For any relative-coordinate distribution $K\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^4)$,
define its translation-invariant two-point bidistribution
$\widetilde K\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4)$ by
$$ \langle\widetilde K,\Psi\rangle =\left\langle K,\ z\longmapsto\int_{\mathbb R^4}\Psi(y+z,y)\,dy\right\rangle, \qquad \Psi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4). $$
The inner function is a test function: its support lies in the difference
of the two compact coordinate projections of $\operatorname{supp}\Psi$;
each derivative in $z$ is the Riemann integral of the corresponding
first-variable derivative of $\Psi$ over a compact rectangle containing
the fixed compact second-variable projection; iterate the real
single-coordinate differentiation rule over every derivative in $z$ and
apply it to both real components, using the compact parameter-integral
differentiation convention of
[[def-qft-regular-polynomial-functional-algebra]].
On each fixed compact support space, every output derivative seminorm is
bounded by the volume of a compact rectangle containing the second-variable
projection times the corresponding source derivative seminorm. The support
of the output lies in the compact difference of the two projections. Thus
this map is continuous on each fixed-support test space, and hence on the LF
test topology [[def-test-function-topology]].
Thus the displayed formula defines a distribution without multiplying
singular distributions. Write $\mathsf H_\mu=\widetilde H_\mu$.

For $F\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbb R^4)$, define its support as the
finite union of the coordinate projections of the supports of its nonconstant
symmetric coefficient kernels. This is a compact set and is presentation
independent by [[lem-qft-tensor-test-function-density]]. For compact
$A,B\subset\mathbb R^4$, write $A\succcurlyeq_{\mathrm{out}} B$ when
$$ x-y\notin C_-:=\{(t,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4:t\le-|\mathbf x|\} \quad\text{for every }x\in A,\ y\in B. $$
This means the first support has no point in the closed causal past of the
second, using the supplier's fixed inertial chart.

For $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal Q_n$ consist of finite coefficient families in
$n$ independent real smooth fields $\phi_i\in C^\infty(X;\mathbb R)$ of the form
$$Q(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n)=\sum_{\mathbf r}\int q_{\mathbf r}(\mathbf x^{(1)},\ldots,\mathbf x^{(n)})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{a=1}^{r_i}\phi_i(x_a^{(i)})\,d\mathbf x,$$
where $\mathbf r=(r_1,\ldots,r_n)\in\mathbb N_0^n$ ranges over a finite set,
$q_{\mathbf r}\in C_c^\infty(X^{r_1}\times\cdots\times X^{r_n};\mathbb C)$,
and each coefficient is symmetric within every block
$\mathbf x^{(i)}=(x_1^{(i)},\ldots,x_{r_i}^{(i)})$.
$X^0$ is a one-point space; an empty product and an integral over no variables
leave the scalar coefficient unchanged. Here $d\mathbf x$ is the product of
the $d^4x_a^{(i)}$ coordinate volume elements over all variables present.
The product
$\prod_iF_i(\phi_i)$ of regular polynomials is in $\mathcal Q_n$.

For $1\le i<j\le n$, define the one-pair contraction
$D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}:\mathcal Q_n\to\mathcal Q_n$ linearly and termwise on
each block coefficient $q_{\mathbf r}$. It is zero if $r_i=0$ or $r_j=0$;
otherwise it has multidegree $\mathbf r-\mathbf e_i-\mathbf e_j$ and
coefficient
$$q'_{\mathbf r-\mathbf e_i-\mathbf e_j}(\mathbf x')=r_i r_j\left\langle\mathsf H_\mu,(x,y)\longmapsto q_{\mathbf r}(\ldots,x,\ldots,y,\ldots)\right\rangle,$$
where $x$ occupies the first variable of block $i$, $y$ occupies the first
variable of block $j$, and the uncontracted variables $\mathbf x'$ are held
as parameters. The result remains symmetric within each remaining block.
The parameter-pairing theorem
[[lem-distribution-pairing-with-smooth-parameter-families]] makes this
coefficient smooth and compactly supported. The factor $r_i r_j$ counts the
choices of one variable from each symmetric block, so this is exactly one
functional derivative in each of the independent field slots followed by
pairing against $\mathsf H_\mu$.

For $r\ge1$, define full symmetrization by
$$\operatorname{Sym}_r h(x_1,\ldots,x_r)=\frac1{r!}\sum_{\pi\in S_r}h(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(r)}),$$
with $\operatorname{Sym}_0$ the identity. For $Q\in\mathcal Q_n$, define
$m_nQ$ by setting $\phi_1=\cdots=\phi_n=\phi$ and replacing each remaining
block coefficient by its full symmetrization across all variables. For a finite-degree $Q$, the
formal exponential is defined coefficientwise by
$$\exp\!\left(\eta\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}\right)Q =\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{\eta^r}{r!}\left(\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}\right)^rQ,$$
which terminates because each contraction lowers total degree by two. The
parameter $\eta$ is formal and fixed by complex conjugation. Define
$$ T_n^H(F_1,\ldots,F_n)(\phi) =m_n\exp\!\left(\eta\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}D_{\mathsf H}^{ij}\right) \prod_{i=1}^nF_i(\phi_i), \qquad T_0^H=1,\quad T_1^H(F)=F. $$
The tensor-product distribution theorem
[[thm-tensor-product-distributions-and-iterated-pairings]] and the
parameter-pairing theorem above make every contraction well defined; no
diagonal product occurs. Symmetry of $\mathsf H_\mu$ makes $T_n^H$ symmetric
in its inputs.

For any $V\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbb R^4)$ and formal coupling $z$,
define
$$ S_z^H(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(iz/\eta)^n}{n!}\,T_n^H(V,\ldots,V) \quad\text{with coefficients in }\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(\mathbb R^4)[\eta,\eta^{-1}]. $$
This is a coefficientwise formal series; the definition asserts no
convergence in $z$, no time-ordered product for singular local functionals,
and no continuum interacting field.

derivations.claim: For real test directions $h,k$, the coefficient of $st$ in $L_g(1+s h+t k)$ is $12\int g(x)h(x)k(x)\,d^4x$, by expanding $(1+s h+t k)^4$. By [F3], this is exactly the pairing of $K_g$ with the product test $h\otimes k$. Thus $K_g$ represents the second derivative on product tests.

For every nonempty fixed compact $K\subseteq X\times X$, choose a compact rectangle $R$ containing its first-coordinate projection. Then $$ |\langle K_g,\Psi\rangle| \le 12\|g\|_\infty\operatorname{vol}(R)\|\Psi\|_\infty \qquad(\operatorname{supp}\Psi\subseteq K), $$ so $K_g$ is continuous on each fixed-support test space and hence on the LF test topology by [F7]. It vanishes on every test supported off the diagonal, so its support is contained there by [F6]. Choose $\rho\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$ with $\rho(0)=1$ using [F5], and set $\Psi(x,y)=g(x)\rho(x-y)$. This is a test function: its support has $x\in\operatorname{supp}g$ and $x-y\in\operatorname{supp}\rho$, so both coordinate projections are compact. Then $$ \langle K_g,\Psi\rangle=12\int_{\mathbb R^4}g(x)^2\,d^4x>0, $$ because a nonzero continuous real function is bounded away from zero on a small ball. Thus $K_g\ne0$.

Suppose $L_g$ had a regular presentation. By [F1], its second derivative at $1$ would have a smooth compactly supported kernel. Its pairings with product tests agree with those of $K_g$ by step 1.1; complex linearity extends agreement to complex product tests, and density [F2] extends it to all tests. Hence the smooth kernel would equal $K_g$ as a distribution. Its support would be contained in the diagonal by step 2.1.

The diagonal has empty interior. A continuous function supported there must vanish: any nonzero value would persist on an open neighborhood not contained in the diagonal. This contradicts $K_g\ne0$ from step 2.1. Therefore $L_g$ has no regular presentation.

By step 4.1, $L_g\notin\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Fact [F8] defines $\star_W$ only on pairs of regular polynomial functionals, and [F9] defines each $T_n^H$ on regular polynomial inputs. Neither operation therefore applies to $L_g$. Any extension across the diagonal is a separate construction and is not proved here.
